## Appendix A Proof of $\Omega C\geq 0$ and comments on $C=0$ vortexability

In this section we prove that the chirality $\Omega$ of vortex geometry is tied to the Chern number of the band and then use the result to understand $C=0$ vortexable bands. There are several ways to show this result, including momentum space band geometry for translationally symmetric systems — which is done in the final section of the main text — as well as the closely related twist angle torus geometry [105, 106] for systems that are placed on a twist-angle torus with arbitrary twisted boundary conditions. Here, however, we will take a bulk position operator point of view33 3 We would like to thank Ruihua Fan for patient help in understanding this perspective, both conceptually and computationally. and use the formula [107, 108, 109]

$$ C=2\pi i\Tr^{\prime}[\mathcal{P}x^{\prime}\mathcal{P},\mathcal{P}y^{\prime}\mathcal{P}]. $$

where $\Tr^{\prime}$ is the trace per unit volume

$$ \Tr^{\prime}A=\lim_{\lvert\Lambda\rvert\to\infty}\frac{1}{\lvert\Lambda\rvert}\tr P_{\Lambda}AP_{\Lambda} $$

where $\Lambda$ labels successively larger regions of real space, $P_{\Lambda}$ projects onto states that vanish outside $\Lambda$ , and we use the volume form $dx^{\prime}\wedge dy^{\prime}$ associated with the coordinates $(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ to measure the volume $\lvert\Lambda\rvert=\int_{\Lambda}dx^{\prime}\wedge dy^{\prime}$ . The trace $\tr$ is the usual dimensionless Hilbert-space trace. Note that some caution is required in using (41) since the trace is over an infinite dimensional space. In particular, the cyclic property only holds when the trace exists and cannot be used on each term of the commutator (40) individually. For systems with lattice translation symmetry we recover the usual formula from (40). In particular we have

$$ [\mathcal{P}x^{\prime}\mathcal{P},\mathcal{P}y^{\prime}\mathcal{P}]=-i\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\mathcal{F}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{k}})\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\bra{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}, $$

such that

$$ \Tr^{\prime}[\mathcal{P}x^{\prime}\mathcal{P},\mathcal{P}y^{\prime}\mathcal{P}]=-i\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathcal{F}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-i\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\mathcal{F}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{k}}), $$

where the Berry curvature $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}$ is defined using the $(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ coordinate system and $V=\int dx^{\prime}\wedge dy^{\prime}$ . For a system on a twist-angle torus we may also use a similar calculation to show that (40) reproduces the expected result44 4 Twist angle boundary conditions are formally equivalent to Bloch boundary conditions if one chooses the entire system to be a single unit cell.

The virtue of (40) is that it makes sense on the infinite plane and is stated in terms of the position operator. We use the coordinates $(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})$ because we will soon plug in the vortex function $\mathsf{z}=x^{\prime}\pm iy^{\prime}$ . As a topological quantity, the Chern number is invariant under of choice of coordinates — though this is not always true for the Hall conductance in states without a charge gap [103].

See Refs. [107, 108, 109] for a careful discussion of Eq. 40. Note that in these references the trace is often written in the equivalent form $\Tr^{\prime}\mathcal{P}[[x,\mathcal{P}][y,\mathcal{P}]]=\Tr^{\prime}\mathcal{P}\left[[x,\mathcal{P}],[y,\mathcal{P}]\right]\mathcal{P}$ to emphasize the role of the position operator as a generalization of a derivative.

We now take $\Omega>0$ such that $\mathsf{z}=x^{\prime}+iy^{\prime}$ and show that $C\geq 0$ . The analogous case of $\Omega<0$ follows straightforwardly. We now compute

$$ \displaystyle C \displaystyle=\pi\Tr^{\prime}[\mathcal{P}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\mathcal{P},\mathcal{P}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}]=\pi\Tr^{\prime}(\mathcal{P}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}-\mathcal{P}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\mathcal{P}) \displaystyle=\pi\Tr^{\prime}\mathcal{P}\mathsf{z}(1-\mathcal{P})\overline{\mathsf{z}}\mathcal{P}=\pi\Tr^{\prime}\mathcal{P}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{Q}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\mathcal{P}\geq 0. $$

where we expanded the commutator, used the vortexability condition $\mathcal{P}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}=\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}$ in the first term, and used the commutativity $[\overline{\mathsf{z}},\mathsf{z}]=0$ of the unprojected vortex functions. The non-negativity comes from the writing $\mathcal{P}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\mathcal{Q}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}=A^{\dagger}A$ as a positive definite operator where $A=\mathcal{Q}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}$ .

### A.1 Vortexable bands with $C=0$

Using the above results, we now shows that $C=0$ vortexable bands are “trivial” in the sense that they do not support FQHE ground states.

If $C=0$ , then by (44), $C=\pi\Tr A^{\dagger}A=\pi\lVert A\rVert^{2}=0$ , so we must have $A=\mathcal{Q}\mathsf{z}\mathcal{P}=0$ . Thus, if $C=0$ then the band is also vortexable with vortex operator $\overline{\mathsf{z}}$ . This makes some sense, as $C=0$ bands intuitively don’t have have a bias towards either chirality. However, this dramatically restricts the wavefunctions of the $C=0$ band. For bands with translation symmetry, for example, it is possible to show that the wavefunctions $\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ may be chosen constant in ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ such that $\mathcal{F}=g_{\mathrm{FS}}=0$ . However, we will instead proceed by characterizing the wavefunctions without reference to the translation symmetric case.

Indeed, since the vortexability condition is linear we have $(\mathsf{z}\pm\overline{\mathsf{z}})\psi=\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{z}\pm\overline{\mathsf{z}})\psi$ such that

$$ {\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}\psi=\mathcal{P}{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}\psi. $$

We may extend this to any analytic function of ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}$ by expanding in a Taylor series. This seems to enable us to construct an infinite number of states in any finite volume. Indeed, consider the attachment

$$ f_{{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime})\ket{\psi}=\mathcal{P}f_{{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime})\ket{\psi},\,\,\,f_{{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\frac{1}{2\pi a^{2}}e^{-\frac{\lVert{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}-{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{0}\rVert^{2}}{2a^{2}}}, $$

Which localizes the wavefunction $\ket{\psi}$ around some position ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ where $\ket{\psi}$ has nonzero density with localization length $a$ . Performing (46) for arbitrarily small $a$ and arbitrarily many positions ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{0}$ seems to enable the construction of an arbitrarily large number of states in a finite volume. The one loophole is that $\ket{\psi}$ , and all other states in the band of interest, may have only finitely many points ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{0}$ with nonzero density, such that the vast majority of attachments (46) simply give zero. This is the case in the tight-binding limit for example, but we find it remarkable that all $C=0$ vortexable bands with finite fully-filled density are exactly in this limit of completely localized states.

We now show that we can describe such bands using a basis of position eigenstates; i.e. the band admits a basis of delta-function localized “Wannier orbitals”. Applying (45) to a basis of states in the band we obtain

$$ {\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}\mathcal{P} $$

and the Hermitian conjugate $\mathcal{P}{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}=\mathcal{P}{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}\mathcal{P}$ . We therefore conclude

$$ [{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime},\mathcal{P}]=0 $$

such that the position operator and the band projector are simultaneously diagonalizable. The band therefore admits a basis in terms of the eigenstates of the position operator as claimed: $\hat{{\boldsymbol{r}}}^{\prime}\ket{\psi_{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{\alpha}\ket{\psi_{\alpha}}$ .

To minimize repulsive interaction energy at fractional filling, we may simply occupy some subset of the orbitals $\ket{\psi_{\alpha}}$ and maximize the minimum distance between occupied orbitals. For instance, one can use a charge-density wave pattern. If, for a given filling factor, the minimum distance between occupied orbitals is $d$ , then the state will be a zero energy ground state of any potential with $V(\lVert{\boldsymbol{r}}\rVert)=0$ for $\lVert{\boldsymbol{r}}\rVert>d$ . This is a much larger class of interactions than the pseudopotential Hamiltonians, which are all ultra-local and only make sense in continuum models.

It is also worth noting that if we start with the fully filled $C=0$ Slater determinant state, then the vortex attachment (9) simply multiplies the wavefunction by a constant. Indeed, the fully filled Slater determinant may be written as the antisymmetric tensor product of position eigenstates such that the vortex operators $\mathsf{z}_{i}$ get replaced by their eigenvalue.

We therefore conclude that vortex attachment in $C=0$ vortexable bands is ineffective in producing fractional quantum Hall states; charge density waves are much more effective at minimizing the interaction energy due to the perfect localization of the single particle states.

## Appendix B Pseudopotential expansions

In this section we argue that the Laughlin-like state

$$ \ket{\Psi^{(2s)}}=\prod_{i<j}(\mathsf{z}_{i}-\mathsf{z}_{j})^{2s}\ket{\Psi} $$

is the ground state for $C\neq 0$ continuum vortexable bands in the limit of short-range interaction potentials. That is, it is an “SRI-GS”. We follow the argument in Ref. [51], which used a real-space version of the Haldane pseudopotentials [71] to argue that the Laughlin state does not crucially depend on angular momentum or rotation symmetry. This argument has recently been applied to chiral twisted bilayer graphene as well [22, 50, 49].

We consider a purely-interacting Hamiltonian projected to the band of interest

$$ H=\mathscr{P}\sum_{i<j}V\left({\boldsymbol{r}}_{i},{\boldsymbol{r}}_{j}\right)\mathscr{P} $$

where $\mathscr{P}=\otimes_{i}\mathcal{P}_{i}$ is the many-body projector to the band of interest. We take $V({\boldsymbol{r}},{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime})=V(|{\boldsymbol{r}}-{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}|)>0$ to be a circularly and translationally symmetric repulsive interaction potential — both for simplicity and because we have a screened-Coulomb-type interaction in mind. The essential piece of the argument below will be power-counting in the short range limit, which may therefore be generalized to any short range repulsive interaction.

We begin by expanding the interaction potential into “pseudopotentials”, written in a real space basis. To understand this expansion, we note that the potential $V({\boldsymbol{r}})=V(r)$ will always be integrated against some matrix element or probability-density of states in the band (for the energy, this will be ultimately be the pair distribution function). Call this function $\Phi({\boldsymbol{r}})$ . The function $\Phi({\boldsymbol{r}})$ generically varies on the scale of the effective magnetic length $\ell$ where $2\pi\ell^{-2}$ is the change in electron density upon fully filling the band. An important exception to this is the tight-binding limit where electrons have a finite average density but are taken to be infinitely localized - this discussion will therefore apply most saliently to continuum models. Note that the tight binding limit is itself an approximation, however, and real electron atomic orbitals tend to have appreciable spread: of the same order as the inter-site distance. We will now proceed assuming $\Phi$ varies on the scale of $\ell$ .

$$ \int d^{2}\,{\boldsymbol{r}}V({\boldsymbol{r}})\Phi({\boldsymbol{r}}). $$

While $\Phi$ is usually not circularly symmetric a priori, we may assume it to be so because it is integrated against $V({\boldsymbol{r}})=V(r)$ . Motivated by Haldane pseudopotentials for short-range interactions, we expand near ${\boldsymbol{r}}=0$ using the Taylor-like expansion for circularly symmetric analytic functions

$$ \Phi({\boldsymbol{r}})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_{n}^{-1}(\nabla^{2n}\Phi)({\boldsymbol{r}}=0)r^{2n}, $$

where $c_{n}=(\nabla^{2n}r^{2n})|_{r=0}=4^{n}(n!)^{2}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}\,V({\boldsymbol{r}})\Phi({\boldsymbol{r}}) \displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_{n}^{-1}((\ell\nabla)^{2n}\Phi)(0)\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}\left(\frac{r}{a_{M}}\right)^{2n}V({\boldsymbol{r}}), $$

where we have inserted factors of $\ell$ to effectively non-dimensionalize $r$ because $\Phi$ varies on the scale of $\ell$ .

The above result may be interpreted as coming from a “pseudopotential” expansion

$$ \displaystyle V({\boldsymbol{r}}) \displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}v_{n}(\ell\nabla)^{2n}\delta({\boldsymbol{r}}) \displaystyle v_{n} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{c_{n}}\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}\left(\frac{r}{\ell}\right)^{2n}V({\boldsymbol{r}})\sim\left(\frac{d}{\ell}\right)^{2n}v_{0}, $$

through the use of integration by parts. Here, $d$ is the range of the interaction. If $d\ll\ell$ the coefficients $v_{n}$ rapidly decrease with $n$ , though they may decrease rapidly regardless due to the extremely rapid growth of $c_{n}=4^{n}(n!)^{2}$ .

### B.1 Ground state in the pseudopotential limit

We now show that the Laughlin-like state $\ket{\Psi^{(2s)}}$ , defined in (49) through attaching $2s$ vortices, is a zero mode under the first $2s-1$ terms of (54) such that the ground state energy scales to zero no-slower-than $d^{4s}$ as $d\to 0$ . 55 5 In the ordinary spin-polarized FQHE an additional vortex from Fermi statistics makes the scaling $d^{4s+2}$ instead, for example. This extra enhancement is not always present. For example it is absent in the spin-singlet $(2s+1,2s+1,2s)$ Halperin states which also arise from vortex attachment.

The energy expectation value is

$$ \displaystyle E \displaystyle=\sum_{i<j}\int V({\boldsymbol{r}}_{i}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{j})d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}_{i}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}_{j} \displaystyle\times\int\lVert\Psi^{(2s)}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})\rVert^{2}\prod_{k\neq i,j}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}_{k} \displaystyle=N\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}V({\boldsymbol{r}}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})G_{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle G^{(2s)}_{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{-}) \displaystyle=(N-1)\int\prod_{k>2}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}_{k}\lVert\Psi^{(2s)}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0},{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}+{\boldsymbol{r}}_{-},{\boldsymbol{r}}_{3},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})\rVert^{2} $$

is the pair distribution function as a function of the relative coordinate ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{-}={\boldsymbol{r}}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ . Above we used that $\lVert\Psi_{2s}(\{\boldsymbol{r}_{i}\})\rVert^{2}$ is a symmetric under permuting the positions of the particles. The vortex attachment (9) implies that

$$ G^{(2s)}_{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{-})=(g^{v}_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})r_{-}^{\mu}r_{-}^{\nu})^{4s}\lambda_{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{-})+\ldots $$

in terms of the vortex metric $g(\boldsymbol{r}_{0})$ defined in the main text. Here the dotted terms vanish with even higher powers of $r_{-}^{\mu}$ and $\lambda_{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{-})$ is some function that we will not be concerned with here, though we ask that it is finite (i.e. not infinite, it is ok if it vanishes) as we would expect in a continuum model with a smooth $G_{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{-})$ .

Using the psuedopotential expansion (54), the energy is then given by

$$ \displaystyle E=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}N\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}} \displaystyle d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}v_{n}(\ell\nabla)^{2n}\delta({\boldsymbol{r}}_{-}) \displaystyle\times\left((g_{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})r_{-}^{\mu}r_{-}^{\nu})^{4s}\lambda({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})+\ldots\right). $$

We then move all derivatives off the delta function through integration by parts, and evaluate the rest of the integrand at ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{-}=0$ in accordance with the delta function. We see that for $n<2s$ there are more powers of $r_{-}^{\mu}$ than derivatives such that the integrand must vanish at ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{-}=0$ . Thus, the energy only receives contributions from $n\geq 2s$ such that the ground state energy is expected to scale as $d^{4s}$ for small $d\ll\ell$ . We expect that other competing states will not be zero modes under all terms with $n<2s$ , such that the state (49) emerges as the ground state as $d\to 0$ .

## Appendix C Strain, Graphene, and Twisted Bilayer Graphene

This Appendix gives details of strain in graphene and TBG that are used in examples in the main text.

*Figure 4: Internal strain of TBG. a. Displacement field $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{r})$ in units of the graphene scale $a_{\mathrm{Gr}}$ . The solid hexagon is a real-space unit cell. b. Magnitude of the displacement field $\left|\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{r})\right|$ . c. Psuedomagnetic field in real space. All data is for $\theta=1.05^{\circ}$ and uses ab initio strain parameters from [84].*

### C.1 Graphene

To set conventions, let $\boldsymbol{R}_{1,2}=(1/2,\mp\sqrt{3}/2)a$ be the lattice of graphene, where $a$ is the graphene lattice constant. Consider graphene where atoms are displaced from their equilibrium positions by $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{r})$ . One can think of this as embedding a 2d crystal of graphene — with regularly spaced atoms — into 3d space in the laboratory. These two frames are called the crystal and laboratory frames respectively, and have coordinates $\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}$ and $\boldsymbol{r}$ [80, 82, 81]. The latter must be used when coupling to all external probes. For instance, electron fields couple as $\boldsymbol{E}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}$ . However, the lattice is only evenly spaced in the crystal frame, making it useful for Fourier transforms. The metric of the crystal frame is trivial, but the embedding makes the metric non-trivial in the laboratory frame:

$$ g_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta_{\mu\nu}+2u_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{r})=e_{\mu}^{a}(\boldsymbol{r})e_{\nu}^{b}(\boldsymbol{r}); $$

where $e_{a\mu}(\boldsymbol{r})=\delta_{a\mu}+\delta_{a}^{\nu}u_{\mu\nu}$ are tetrads giving an local orthonormal basis [80] and $\quad u_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{r})=\frac{1}{2}[\partial_{\mu}u_{\nu}+\partial_{\nu}u_{\mu}]$ is the strain tensor in terms of the atomic displacements $u_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ .

At first order in a derivative expansion, the low energy continuum model of strained graphene is:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{h}_{\text{strained graphene}} \displaystyle=v_{F}\int d^{2}\boldsymbol{r}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}e_{a}^{\mu}\sigma^{a}(-i\partial_{\mu}-\mathcal{A}_{\mu}(\boldsymbol{r}))\hat{\psi}(\boldsymbol{r}), \displaystyle\mathcal{A} \displaystyle=\frac{\beta}{2a}(u_{xx}-u_{yy},-2u_{xy}), $$

where the strain gauge field $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}$ is determined by the elastic coefficient $\beta=\partial\ln t(d)/\partial\ln d\big|_{d=a}$ in terms of the hopping matrix element $t$ at separation $d$ , and $v_{F}$ is the Fermi velocity [110]. Remarkably, the Hamiltonian takes the form (60) in both frames at this order in derivatives, though it differs at second order in derivatives, where a spin connection enters [82].

### C.2 Strained Twisted Bilayer Graphene

At twist angle $\theta$ , the unstrained moiré reciprocal lattice is $\boldsymbol{g}_{1,2}=(2\pi/\sqrt{3},\pm 2\pi)L_{M}^{-1}$ where $L_{M}=[2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}]^{-1}a$ in terms of the graphene unit cell. A standard model for the low energy Hamiltonian (in the $K$ -valley) is [50]:

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}_{\mathrm{TBG}}(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}-iv_{F}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\nabla}&T(\boldsymbol{r})\\
T(\boldsymbol{r})^{\dagger}&-iv_{F}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\nabla}\end{pmatrix}_{UL}, \displaystyle\quad T(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=w_{AB}\begin{bmatrix}\kappa U_{0}(\boldsymbol{r})&U_{1}(\boldsymbol{r})\\
\overline{U_{1}(-\boldsymbol{r})}&\kappa U_{0}(\boldsymbol{r})\end{bmatrix}_{AB}, $$

where “UL” and “AB” specify layer and sublattice blocks respectively. We take $w_{AB}=$110\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ , and $0\leq\kappa\leq 1$ is the chiral parameter.

Here, $-iv_{F}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\boldsymbol{\nabla}$ is the standard continuum model of graphene for the top and bottom layers. Rotations of the Pauli matrices are neglected, ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{\pm\theta/2}\to{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$ , due to their negligable effect at small twist angles. Though for the $\kappa=0$ chiral model of interest they may also be removed by a unitary transformation [38].

The functions

$$ \displaystyle U_{0}(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}_{1}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}+e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}_{2}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}+e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}_{3}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}, \displaystyle U_{1}(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}_{1}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}+e^{-2\pi i/3}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}_{2}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}+e^{-4\pi i/3}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}_{3}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}} $$

encode the tunneling between layers. The tunneling wavevectors, which connect the Dirac points in each layer, are ${\boldsymbol{q}}_{1}=k_{\theta}(0,-1)$ and ${\boldsymbol{q}}_{2,3}=k_{\theta}\left(\pm\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)$ , where $k_{\theta}=\frac{4\pi}{3L_{M}}$ and $\boldsymbol{g}_{1,2}={\boldsymbol{q}}_{2,3}-{\boldsymbol{q}}_{1}$ .

We now consider the effect of strain. Experimental samples of TBG possess both external and internal strain. Externally imposed strain (e.g. from the substrate) distorts the moiré unit cell itself, and can significantly shift the energetics and ground state phases of the system [111, 112]. Internal strain, by contrast, leaves the moiré unit cell unchanged and expands the AB regions while shrinking the AA regions. As internal strain is caused by the action of one graphene sheet on the other, it is necessarily present even in pristine and completely isolated samples. Physically, this is because Bernal (AB) stacking is energetically preferable to AA stacking. Therefore TBG locally displaces towards Bernal stacking everywhere except the centers of the AA regions, where the lattice instead buckles out of plane. This effect has been carefully studied in ab initio calculations and observed in experiments. As both AB regions growing and AA regions buckling serve to reduce the AA tunnelling, it is often modelled phenomenologically by reducing the chiral ratio from $\kappa=1$ to $\kappa=0.5-0.8$ .

Here we take a more microscopic perspective. We consider a moiré-periodic displacement field [83]

$$ \boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{r})=\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{r})^{+}-\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{r})^{-}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{g}}\boldsymbol{u}_{\boldsymbol{g}}e^{i\boldsymbol{g}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}} $$

which is equal and opposite between the two layers $\pm$ . We take parameters $\boldsymbol{u}_{\boldsymbol{g}}$ from Ref. [83] (see also [89]). This, in turn, induces a moiré-periodic pseudo-vector potential

$$ \mathcal{A}^{\pm}(\boldsymbol{r})=\frac{\beta}{2a}(u_{xx}^{\pm}-u_{yy}^{\pm},-2u_{xy}^{\pm}),\quad\boldsymbol{u}_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{r})^{\pm}=\frac{1}{2}[\partial_{r_{\mu}}u_{\nu}^{\pm}+\partial_{r_{\nu}}u_{\mu}^{\pm}], $$

and psuedo-magnetic field $\mathcal{B}=d\mathcal{A}$ , shown in Fig. 4. We note this microscopically realistic psuedomagnetic field averages to zero, but has peaks of $\sim$80\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$$ [83] — a significant perturbation.

The Hamiltonian for (internally) strained TBG is therefore

$$ \hat{H}(\boldsymbol{r})=\hat{H}_{\mathrm{TBG}}(\boldsymbol{r})+v_{F}\begin{pmatrix}\sigma^{\mu}\mathcal{A}_{\mu}^{+}(\boldsymbol{r})&0\\
0&\sigma^{\mu}\mathcal{A}_{\mu}^{-}(\boldsymbol{r})\end{pmatrix}. $$

Permuting the layer and sublattice indices, we can write this as

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\kappa T_{0}(\boldsymbol{r})&D_{\mathrm{TBG}}^{\dagger}\\
D_{\mathrm{TBG}}&\kappa T_{0}(\boldsymbol{r})\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle T_{0}(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}0&U_{0}(\boldsymbol{r})\\
\overline{U_{0}(-\boldsymbol{r})}\end{bmatrix}, \displaystyle D_{\mathrm{TBG}} \displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}2\chi_{+}^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}})(-i\partial_{\mu}+\mathcal{A}_{\mu}^{+})&\alpha U_{1}(\boldsymbol{r})\\
\alpha U_{1}(-\boldsymbol{r})&2\chi_{-}^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}})(-i\partial_{\mu}+\mathcal{A}_{\mu}^{-})\end{bmatrix}, $$

where $\chi_{\pm}^{\mu}(\boldsymbol{r})=\tfrac{1}{2}[e_{1\pm}^{\mu}+ie_{2\pm}^{\mu}]$ . Replacing $\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{r})\to\alpha_{s}\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{r})$ and taking $\kappa\to 0$ gives Eq. (17) in the main text.

Eq. (66) retains the symmetries of unstrained TBG, including $C_{3z}$ , $C_{2x}$ , and particle-hole symmetries. This is because we consider strains which are equal and opposite in the two layers, and because the displacement field $\boldsymbol{u}^{\pm}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is itself $C_{3}$ and $C_{2x}$ symmetric (Fig. 4) — and hence $\mathcal{A}(\boldsymbol{r})$ is as well.

## Appendix D Review of traditional band geometry

This section will review “traditional” results on band geometry and its relationship to the FQHE. We start off by recalling the definitions of band geometry, and the key results on how to mimic a Landau level from conditions on band geometry. One of these conditions — the determinant condition — can be understood as a $\boldsymbol{k}$ -dependent generalization of the trace condition. However, we immediately argue that the determinant condition is not physically meaningful in the context of FQHE physics. Our treatment is entirely self-contained.

For ease of referencing, we copy the band geometry definitions from the main text below.

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\sum_{a}\bra{\partial^{k_{\nu}}u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}b}}Q(\boldsymbol{k})\ket{\partial^{k_{\mu}}u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}, \displaystyle Q({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=1-\sum_{a}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}\bra{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}} \displaystyle g_{\mathrm{FS}}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\Re\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}}),\quad\mathcal{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}=-\frac{1}{2}\Im\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}}). $$

### D.1 Landau Level Mimicry

The FS metric and Berry curvature for the LLL are given by

$$ g_{\text{FS, }0}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\frac{1}{2}\ell^{2}\delta^{\mu\nu},\qquad\mathcal{F}_{0}=\ell^{2} $$

where $\ell$ is the magnetic length [32, 50]. Roy showed that the Girvin-Macdonald-Platzmann algebra [36] of density operators holds if the Fubini-Study metric and the Berry curvature are the same as those of the LLL [37]. If, additionally, the band is flat with Chern number $\pm 1$ , then the many-body problem of electrons interacting in the LLL is fully reproduced and we expect to obtain an FCI in the band of interest.

While a full mimicking of the LLL band geometry is required for Roy’s result, partial results may or may not be sufficient. Each of the following conditions have been proposed as potential conditions, perhaps sufficient, or necessary, or both, for ideality (see e.g. [27]).

- (G1) The Berry curvature is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent.

- (G2) The Fubini-Study metric is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent.

- (G3) The determinant inequality $\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\sqrt{\det g_{\mathrm{FS}}}\geq\pi\lvert C\rvert$ is saturated (determinant condition).

- (G4) The trace inequality $\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\tr g_{\mathrm{FS}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\geq 2\pi\lvert C\rvert$ is saturated (trace condition).

As the geometry of the LLL (68) obeys $\tr g_{\text{FS, }0}(\boldsymbol{k})=\ell^{2}=\mathcal{F}_{0}$ and $\sqrt{\det g_{\text{FS, }0}(\boldsymbol{k})}=\ell^{2}/2$ , all four conditions are exactly satisfied. The ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independence of $g_{FS}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ originates from continuous magnetic translation symmetry, and the relationship (G4) between the FS metric and the Berry curvature can be understood through vortexability, as discussed in the main text.

We note that there are relationships between the above conditions that we will now review. The inequality in condition (G3) comes from noting that $\tilde{\eta}$ is a positive semidefinite matrix and computing

$$ \det\tilde{\eta}=\det g_{\mathrm{FS}}-\frac{1}{4}\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert^{2}\geq 0. $$

The inequality in (G3) then follows from taking a square root, integrating over $\boldsymbol{k}$ , and applying the fact

$$ \int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert\geq\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathcal{F}=2\pi C. $$

Therefore the inequality in (G3) is saturated if and only if $\det\tilde{\eta}=0$ and $\mathcal{F}$ does not change sign. The inequality in (G4) then follows by applying the arithmetic mean-geometric mean (AM-GM) inequality on the real & positive eigenvalues of $g_{FS}$ , which yields $\tr g_{\mathrm{FS}}\geq 2\sqrt{\det g_{\mathrm{FS}}}$ . The trace condition (G4) therefore implies the determinant condition (G3) and is satisfied if and only if $g^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{FS}}=\pm\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{F}\delta^{\mu\nu}$ such that the AM-GM inequality is saturated for the eigenvalues of $g$ and $\mathcal{F}$ does not change sign. Additionally, this implies that (G1) and (G4) together imply (G2). Thus, if (G1) and (G4) are satisfied, all four conditions are.

There is a rich structure associated with conditions (G3-4). In particular, the determinant condition is saturated if and only if the Berry curvature does not change sign 66 6 Note that sign changes of the Berry curvature are somewhat singular when the determinant condition is satisfied because they come with a degenerate metric $\det g_{\mathrm{FS}}=0$ , see (69). If one only demands $4\det g_{\mathrm{FS}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\mathcal{F}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{2}$ for all ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ , rather than $\int d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\sqrt{\det g_{\mathrm{FS}}}=\pi\lvert C\rvert$ , then sign changes of the Berry curvature are allowed. and there is a complex vector $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ that varies smoothly with ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ that satisfies the following equivalent conditions.

- (D1) The vector $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is a zero mode of the quantum metric: $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=0$ .

- (D2) The periodic wavefunctions satisfy $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}=0$ with $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}=\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\partial^{k_{\mu}}$ .

- (D3) The Bloch wavefunctions satisfy $\mathsf{z}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=\mathcal{P}\mathsf{z}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ where $\mathsf{z}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})r^{\mu}$ .

The trace condition (G4) is a special case of the determinant condition with $g^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{FS}}\propto\delta^{\mu\nu}$ and corresponds to the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -indepdenent $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\begin{pmatrix}1&i\end{pmatrix}^{T}$ such that $\mathsf{z}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=z=x+iy$ .

The condition (D3) is a weaker version of vortexability where the vortex function is allowed to be ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ dependent. To our knowledge, this weaker vortexability condition does not enable us to make any pseudopotential arguments. Furthermore, we will soon argue that ideality conditions for the FQHE should be invariant under forgetting translation symmetry, and the determinant condition is not — unless $\omega_{\mu}$ is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent (see Sec. D.3). A generic ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent $\omega_{\mu}$ is a mild generalization of the trace condition; the usual trace condition may be recovered by the linear transformation on ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ that makes the Fubini-Study metric proportional to the identity matrix.

Let us now prove the equivalence of (D1-3) to the determinant condition with single-sign Berry curvature. We first prove this for (D1) and then show (D1) $\iff$ (D2), (D2) $\iff$ (D3). Note that the determinant condition is satisfied if and only if $\det\tilde{\eta}({\boldsymbol{k}})=0$ for all ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ and the Berry curvature has the same sign throughout the BZ; see the discussion around (69), (70). Then the condition $\det\tilde{\eta}(\boldsymbol{k})=0$ is satisfied if and only if there is a zero mode $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=0$ .

To show (D1) $\iff$ (D2) we compute

$$ \displaystyle\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\omega_{\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})} \displaystyle=\sum_{a}\bra{\omega_{\nu}\partial^{k_{\nu}}u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\ket{\omega_{\mu}\partial^{k_{\mu}}u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}} \displaystyle=\sum_{a}\lVert Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\partial_{\mathsf{k}}u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}\rVert^{2}. $$

The vanishing of the left and right hand sides are equivalent to (D1) and (D2) respectively.

We finish by showing (D2) $\iff$ (D3) using an argument that is very similar to that of the trace condition vortexability in the main text; we include the details here for completeness. We begin with the product rule

$$ -i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}=\hat{{\boldsymbol{r}}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}+e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{r}}}(-i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}})\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}. $$

Acting with $\mathcal{Q}:=1-\mathcal{P}=1-\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}\bra{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ annihilates the left hand side of Eq. (72), giving

$$ \mathcal{Q}{\boldsymbol{r}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}=\mathcal{Q}ie^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{a}}. $$

For clarity, the projector $\mathcal{Q}$ acts on Bloch periodic wavefunctions $\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ and contains a sum over ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ , whereas $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})$ acts on periodic wavefunctions, appears in the definition of quantum geometry (67), and contains no sum over ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ . Since $\bra{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ vanishes for ${\boldsymbol{k}}\neq{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}$ by translation symmetry, we have $\mathcal{Q}e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}=e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}Q({\boldsymbol{k}}){\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}$ , a rewriting of the right hand side of (73). We therefore have

$$ \mathcal{Q}r^{\mu}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=e^{i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}Q({\boldsymbol{k}})i\partial^{k_{\mu}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}, $$

such that dotting each side with $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ gives

$$ \mathcal{Q}\mathsf{z}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0\iff Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}} $$

which establishes the equivalence between (D2) and (D3).

In Ref. [31], the condition (D2) was interpreted in the context of Kähler geometry. In particular, the periodic wavefunctions $\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ determine a map from the Brillouin Zone to complex projective space (such that the unphysical phase of the wavefunction is quotiented away). This map is a holomorphic function of the complex coordinate $\mathsf{k}$ , where $\mathsf{k}$ solves the Beltrami equation $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\mathsf{k}=0$ , if and only if the condition (D2) is satisfied with a “non-degenerate” $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . By non-degenerate we mean that the metric $g^{(\omega)}_{\mu\nu}=\Re\overline{\omega_{\mu}}\omega_{\nu}$ is non-degenerate (i.e. bounded with no zero modes). It is possible to show that this is the case if the Fubini-Study metric is bounded with no zero modes, as $g_{\mathrm{FS}}\propto(g^{(\omega)})^{-1}$ , but this will not be important for us.

Through such a holomorphic map, the Kähler structure of complex projective space is pulled back to the Brillouin Zone and the pull backs of the Riemannian metric and symplectic form of complex projective space may be identified as the Fubini-Study metric and the Berry curvature respectively [31].

### D.2 Holomorphic Bloch wavefunctions

The determinant and trace conditions enable us to perform a gauge transformation, that is in general non-unitary and non-periodic,

$$ \ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}\to\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}=S({\boldsymbol{k}})\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}, $$

with matrix multiplication in band indices, such that the new wavefunction is a holomorphic function of the coordinate $\mathsf{k}$ [31]

$$ \overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}=\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\partial^{k_{\mu}}\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}=0. $$

In this section we will explicitly construct such an $S({\boldsymbol{k}})$ .

While $S({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is in general non-unitary and non-periodic, this is a powerful result that we will use to prove a uniqueness result on vortex functions (Prop. 3 below). Indeed, as discussed in the main text, there is always a coordinate frame for which vortexable bands satisfy (D1) and (D2) with a ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent $\omega_{\mu}$ (see also Prop 2). We imagine $\mathsf{k}$ -holomorphicity will be a future calculational tool as well for working with such bands, so we elaborate on how to choose such a gauge here.

To obtain (77) we will combine (D2), $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}=0$ , a gauge invariant statement, with a choice of $S({\boldsymbol{k}})$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\underbrace{(S_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}})}_{\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}} \displaystyle=[Q({\boldsymbol{k}})+P({\boldsymbol{k}})]\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}(S_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}) \displaystyle=P({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}(S_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}})=0, \displaystyle\iff(\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}+i\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}})S_{\boldsymbol{k}}=0, $$

where $\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\omega_{\mu}A^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is a matrix-valued function of ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ , and $A^{\mu}_{ab}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-i\bra{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}b}}\partial^{k_{\mu}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ is the Berry connection. We assume the Berry connection is smooth in ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ (and therefore not periodic under translations by reciprocal lattice vectors). Such a gauge choice is always possible.

We will solve the right side of (78) with an explicit ansatz for $S_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ . We begin by noting the identity

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}W[f]({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{k}}), \displaystyle W[f]({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\frac{f(\mathsf{k}-\zeta)}{\zeta}d\overline{\zeta}d\zeta. $$

Note that $f$ does not need to be holomorphic. For completeness we pause to prove (79). We excise an arbitrarily small disk $D_{\varepsilon}$ centered at the origin with radius $\varepsilon$ (where the denominator becomes singular) and compute, using Stokes’ theorem

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}W[f](\mathsf{k}) \displaystyle=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\mathbb{C}-D_{\varepsilon}}\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\frac{f(\mathsf{k}-\zeta)}{\zeta}d\overline{\zeta}\wedge d{\zeta} \displaystyle=-\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\mathbb{C}-D_{\varepsilon}}\frac{\overline{\partial}_{\zeta}f(\mathsf{k}-\zeta)}{\zeta}d\overline{\zeta}\wedge d{\zeta} \displaystyle=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial D_{\varepsilon}}\frac{f(\mathsf{k}-\zeta)}{\zeta}d{\zeta} \displaystyle=f(\mathsf{k})\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{D_{\varepsilon}}\frac{d\zeta}{\zeta} \displaystyle=f(\mathsf{k}). $$

To apply Stokes’ theorem, we used the differential-form calculation $d(\frac{f}{\zeta}d\zeta)=\frac{\partial_{\overline{\zeta}}f}{\zeta}d\overline{\zeta}\wedge d\zeta$ away from $\zeta=0$ . The negative sign in the second line originates from the chain rule and disappears in the third line due to change in orientation from $\partial(\mathbb{C}-D_{\varepsilon})$ to $\partial{D_{\varepsilon}}$ . Finally, we pulled $f(\mathsf{k}-\zeta)\approx f(\mathsf{k})$ out of the integral using the $\varepsilon\to 0$ limit in which the integral domain involves arbitrarily small $\zeta$ .

We now write the ansatz

$$ S_{\boldsymbol{k}}=1-iW[h]({\boldsymbol{k}}) $$

under which we may solve (78) for $h$ iteratively:

$$ \displaystyle h=\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}-i\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}W[h], \displaystyle=\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}-i\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}W[\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}]+(-i)^{2}\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}W[\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}W[\overline{A}_{\mathsf{k}}]]+\ldots. $$

We may view the above solution as a generalization of the path ordered exponential used to solve real first order matrix differential equations. To show convergence of Eq. (82), we first show that it converges locally and then patch together local solutions. We may partition the total space $\mathbb{C}$ (that $\mathsf{k}$ lives on) with an open cover of sets $U_{i}$ for $U_{i}$ arbitrarily small. Note that on a set $U_{i}$ of diameter $\delta$ we have $\lvert W[f]\rvert\leq\delta\max_{U_{i}}\lvert f\rvert$ , such that (82) converges for sufficiently small $\delta$ . It remains to patch the solutions on the various $U_{i}$ together, but there is no obstruction to this because $\mathbb{C}$ is contractible. Explicitly, on intersections $U_{i}\cap U_{j}$ , the solutions differ by a holomorphic matrix: $S_{i}({\boldsymbol{k}})=F_{ij}(\mathsf{k})S_{j}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . To see this, apply $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}$ to $F_{ij}=S_{j}^{-1}S_{i}$ and use (78). The collection of matrices $F_{ij}(\mathsf{k})$ may be interpreted as transition functions for a holomorphic vector bundle over $\mathbb{C}$ . But since $\mathbb{C}$ is contractible, there exists trivializing functions $g_{i}(\mathsf{k})$ such that $F_{ij}(\mathsf{k})=\overline{g_{i}(\mathsf{k})}g_{j}(\mathsf{k})$ . Then the matrix $S_{\boldsymbol{k}}=g_{i}(\mathsf{k})S_{i}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is independent of the patch $i$ , and is thus globally defined.

We have now shown the existence of a complexified gauge $S_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ so that $\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}=S_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ is $\mathsf{k}$ -holomorphic.

### D.3 The determinant condition is not folding invariant

One filtration technique on natural ideal conditions for fractional quantum Hall states is invariance under the process of “forgetting” translation symmetry. Indeed, opting to use the maximally sized Brillouin zone is a choice; the fractional quantum Hall effect is just as likely to occur if we use a different description to describe the single particle wavefunctions.

Another way to motivate this requirement is that the FQHE is stable under weak perturbations, and so the single particle band-geometric heuristics should not drastically change under such perturbations, for example an arbitrarily weak perturbation that breaks translation symmetry to a subgroup and folds the Brillouin Zone onto itself.

Consider enlarging the real space unit cell area by a factor of $M$ . This increases the number of bands from $N$ to $MN$ and causes $M$ vectors ${\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m}$ in the original first Brillouin Zone to become reciprocal lattice vectors, such that the new first Brillouin Zone is $M$ times smaller. This “folding” of the Brillouin Zone corresponds to a new labeling of the single particle wavefunctions

$$ \ket{\psi^{f}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}(a,m)}}=\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+m{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m},a}}. $$

for ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ in the folded Brillouin zone, which is $M$ times smaller than the original Brillouin Zone. Correspondingly

$$ \ket{u^{f}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}(a,m)}}=e^{i{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+m{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m},a}}. $$

The “forgotten” translation symmetry implies that $\braket{\tilde{u}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}(a,m)}|\tilde{u}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}(a^{\prime},m^{\prime})}}=0$ for $m\neq m^{\prime}$ , even if ${\boldsymbol{k}}\neq{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}$ . The new quantum metric can therefore be computed as

$$ \tilde{\eta}_{f}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\sum_{m}\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m}) $$

such that it is now periodic in the new first Brillouin Zone.

We will now show that the determinant condition is not invariant under the operation of forgetting translation symmetry and folding the Brillouin Zone, except when $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent. In this case the trace condition in linearly transformed coordinates is satisfied. We use condition (D1): $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})\tilde{\eta}^{\mu\nu}({\boldsymbol{k}})=0$ . For this to be true for $\tilde{\eta}^{f}(\boldsymbol{k})$ , which is a sum of positive definite matrices $\tilde{\eta}({\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m})$ , we must have that the zero modes $\omega({\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m})$ all coincide. If we consider a thermodynamically large system and forget all translation symmetry, then the vectors ${\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m}$ form a dense subset of the Brillouin Zone such that we must have a ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent $\omega_{\mu}$ as claimed.

Note that our result — that the determinant condition is folding invariant if and only if $\omega_{\mu}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is constant — was first obtained by Refs. [31, 32] from a mathematical perspective of satisfying the determinant condition on the twist angle torus. Their twist angle torus effectively emerges when we forget all translation symmetry, such that the entire system is a single unit cell and the Bloch boundary conditions and the twist angle boundary conditions may be identified.

## Appendix E Uniqueness of the vortex function

This section is devoted to proving a uniqueness result on vortexable bands: Prop. 3. We show that under mild assumptions — a ‘generic’ continuum model with discrete translation symmetry — vortex functions are unique. Some restriction on the electron density is necessary to avoid pathological cases: the vortex function may take arbitrary values where the band has no density. For example, in the strict tight binding limit only the values of the vortex function at atomic sites matter. We will take the electron density to be finite continuous and almost never zero, which is sufficient for our proof and is the typical situation in continuum models. The assumption of lattice translation symmetry can perhaps be weakened, though we emphasize that the unit cell of the lattice can be arbitrarily large and we do not restrict the number of Bloch bands. We expect most condensed matter systems to be translation symmetric in the limit where the unit cell is taken to be thermodynamically large.

We will have to prove some prerequisite results before directly addressing uniqueness. We start with a simple result on the form of vortexable bands with translation symmetry.

#### Proposition 1.

Consider a vortexable band with discrete translation symmetry: ${\boldsymbol{r}}\to{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}$ and $\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ . Then $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\omega_{\mu}a^{\mu}$ for some complex vector $\omega_{\mu}$ .

#### Proof.

From $\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ we conclude that $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\beta_{\boldsymbol{a}}$ for an ${\boldsymbol{a}}$ dependent constant $\beta_{\boldsymbol{a}}$ . Iterating translations, we find $\beta_{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}}=\beta_{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}}+\beta_{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}}$ such that $\beta$ is a linear function on the lattice. We may therefore write $\beta_{\boldsymbol{a}}=\omega_{\mu}a^{\mu}$ for some complex-valued vector $\omega_{\mu}$ . ∎

We will find it convenient to use a unit-cell averaged version of the vortex geometry to characterize $\omega_{\mu}$ .

#### Lemma 1.

Consider a vortexable band with discrete translation symmetry $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\omega_{\mu}a^{\mu}$ (Prop. 1). We have

$$ \int_{\mathrm{uc}}\Omega({\boldsymbol{r}})d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}=\Omega^{(\omega)}A_{\mathrm{uc}}=-i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\overline{\omega_{\mu}}\omega_{\nu}A_{\mathrm{uc}}. $$

Here $\Omega=-i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{z}$ is the vortex chirality, the integral is over the unit cell, $A_{\mathrm{uc}}$ is the unit cell area, and $\Omega^{(\omega)}=-i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\overline{\omega}_{\mu}\omega_{\nu}$ . Furthermore, the metric $g^{(\omega)}_{\mu\nu}=\Re\overline{\omega}_{\mu}\omega_{\nu}$ is non-degenerate ( $\det g^{(\omega)}\neq 0)$ .

#### Proof.

First we write $\Omega$ as a curl

$$ \displaystyle\Omega \displaystyle=-i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\overline{\mathsf{z}}\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{z}=-i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}(\overline{\mathsf{z}}\partial_{\nu}\mathsf{z})=\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}\times{\boldsymbol{A}}, \displaystyle A_{\mu} \displaystyle=-i\overline{\mathsf{z}}\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}, $$

such that we may apply Stokes’ theorem

$$ \int_{\mathrm{uc}}\Omega d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}=\oint_{\partial\mathrm{uc}}{\boldsymbol{A}}\cdot d{\boldsymbol{r}}, $$

where the line integral is taken counter-clockwise around the parallelogram defined by the points ${\boldsymbol{r}},{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2},{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}$ . We may group the paths associated with the opposite sides of the parallelogram and use the boundary condition $\overline{\mathsf{z}}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\overline{\mathsf{z}}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\overline{\omega}_{\mu}a^{\mu}$ . We then obtain

$$ \displaystyle\oint_{\partial\mathrm{uc}}{\boldsymbol{A}}\cdot d{\boldsymbol{r}} \displaystyle=-i\int_{{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}}^{{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}}\overline{\omega}_{\mu}a_{1}^{\mu}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}\mathsf{z}\cdot d{\boldsymbol{r}} \displaystyle-i\int_{{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}}^{{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}_{2}}\overline{\omega}_{\nu}a_{2}^{\nu}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}\mathsf{z}\cdot d{\boldsymbol{r}} \displaystyle=-i\overline{\omega}_{\mu}a_{1}^{\mu}\omega_{\nu}a_{2}^{\nu}-\overline{\omega}_{\mu}a_{2}^{\mu}\omega_{\nu}a_{1}^{\nu} \displaystyle=-i(\overline{\omega}_{\mu}\omega_{\nu}-\overline{\omega}_{\nu}\omega_{\mu})a_{1}^{\mu}a_{2}^{\nu} \displaystyle=-i\varepsilon^{\rho\sigma}\overline{\omega}_{\rho}\omega_{\sigma}A_{\mathrm{uc}}, $$

where we used that two-dimensional antisymmetric matrices $B_{\mu\nu}$ are proportional to $\varepsilon_{\mu\nu}$ and therefore satisfy $B_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{\rho\sigma}B_{\rho\sigma}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu}$ . We also identified $\varepsilon_{\mu\nu}a_{1}^{\mu}a_{2}^{\nu}=A_{\mathrm{uc}}$ .

For the last part of the proposition we use the rank one Hermitian matrix $\eta^{(\omega)}_{\mu\nu}=\overline{\omega}_{\mu}\omega_{\nu}$ . Computing $0=\det\eta^{(\omega)}=\det g^{(\omega)}-\lvert\Omega^{(\omega)}\rvert^{2}$ then implies that $\det g^{(\omega)}\neq 0$ .

∎

#### Proposition 2.

Suppose we have a vortexable band with discrete translation symmetry ${\boldsymbol{r}}\to{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}$ , where the vortex function satisfies $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\omega_{\mu}a^{\mu}$ (Prop 1). Define periodic wavefunctions

$$ \ket{u^{\prime}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}, $$

using a periodic diffeomorphism ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})={\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})+{\boldsymbol{a}}$ . We may choose ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ such that

- 1. $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0$ where $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}=\omega_{\mu}\partial^{k_{\mu}}$

- 2. There exists a gauge choice $\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}=S_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ , where $S_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ is invertible but generically non-unitary, so that

$$ \overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}=0, $$

(91) i.e. the periodic wavefunctions are holomorphic functions of $\mathsf{k}$ .

Here $\mathsf{k}$ is a linear function of $\boldsymbol{k}$ such that $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\mathsf{k}=0$ .

#### Proof.

The coordinate system ${\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is obtained by first choosing “non-periodic” coordinates ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{\mathsf{z}}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ where $\mathsf{z}=x_{\mathsf{z}}+iy_{\mathsf{z}}$ using the fact that $\mathsf{z}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a diffeomorphism [see below Eq. (5)]. These coordinates satisfy

$$ r_{\mathsf{z}}^{\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=r^{\mu}_{\mathsf{z}}({\boldsymbol{r}})+J^{\mu}_{\nu}a^{\nu} $$

where $J^{x}_{\mu}=\Re\omega_{\mu}$ and $J^{y}_{\mu}=\Im\omega_{\mu}$ . We have $J^{T}J=g^{(\omega)}$ , and $\det g^{(\omega)}\neq 0$ (Lemma 1), so $J$ is invertible. We then define $(r^{\prime})^{\mu}=(J^{-1})^{\mu}_{\nu}r_{\mathsf{z}}^{\nu}$ , whereupon

$$ {\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})={\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{r}})+{\boldsymbol{a}} $$

as claimed.

With this choice $\mathsf{z}=\omega_{\mu}r^{\prime\mu}$ . Then the equivalence (D1) $\iff$ (D2) $\iff$ (D3) in Sec. D, applied to the wavefunctions $\ket{u^{\prime}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}}\ket{\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ , implies that $\omega_{\mu}$ is a left zero mode of the quantum metric and $Q({\boldsymbol{k}})\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}=0$ . Next, the non-degeneracy $\det g^{(\omega)}\neq 0$ together with the discussion of Sec. D.2 enables us to construct an $S_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ such that $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}$ = 0. ∎

A canonical choice of holomorphic coordinate $\mathsf{k}$ is

$$ \mathsf{k}=i\left(\Omega^{(\omega)}\right)^{-1}\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\omega_{\mu}k_{\nu}, $$

where $\Omega^{(\omega)}=-i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\overline{\omega}_{\mu}\omega_{\nu}$ from Lemma 1. The definition (94) was chosen so that

$$ \overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\mathsf{k}=\omega_{\mu}\partial^{k_{\mu}}\mathsf{k}=0,\qquad\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\mathsf{k}=\overline{\omega}_{\mu}\partial^{k_{\mu}}\mathsf{k}=1. $$

A conceptual point worth emphasizing is that vortexability $\mathsf{z}\ket{\psi}=\mathcal{P}\mathsf{z}\ket{\psi}$ remarkably does not depend on the Hilbert space inner product $\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle$ — despite its dependence on the orthogonal projector $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}(\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle)$ . Indeed, the existence of a gauge where $\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}=0$ is satisfied is completely independent of the Hilbert space inner product, its equivalence to vortexability notwithstanding.

We need one last technical Lemma before the uniqueness result. Namely, we need to understand some properties of the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -space zeros of wavefunctions in the holomorphic gauge. The existence of such zeros and their relation to the Chern number was shown by Ref. [49] for a single Bloch band. Since vortexable “bands” can contain many Bloch bands, we must prove this result for multiple bands. This follows by passing to wavefunctions

$$ \mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1}\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})=\varepsilon^{a_{1},\ldots a_{N}}\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}a_{1}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1})\ldots\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}a_{N}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{N}). $$

in the “determinant-line-bundle” associated to the vector bundle of Bloch wavefunctions $\mathsf{u}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}$ .

#### Lemma 2.

Consider a vortexable band with discrete translation symmetry $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\omega_{\mu}a^{\mu}$ (Prop. 1), such that there are holomorphic periodic wavefunctions $\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}$ (Prop. 2) where $\mathsf{k}$ is given by (94). Then the Chern number is given by the contour integral around the boundary of the Brillouin Zone

$$ C=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial\mathrm{BZ}}\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\ln\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1}\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})d\mathsf{k}=N_{z} $$

where $\partial_{\mathsf{k}}$ and $\mathsf{k}$ are given in (94), (95) such that $\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\mathsf{k}=1$ . The integral counts the number of ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -space zeros $N_{z}$ , multiplicities included, of $\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}$ defined in (96).

#### Proof.

We first show that the integral counts the number of zeros. Note that the logarithm $\log\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}$ , as well as $\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}$ , are $\mathsf{k}$ -holomorphic functions where they are defined (away from zeros of the logarithm). Thus we may use Cauchy’s integral theorem to deform the path of the integral as we please, as long as we don’t cross any zeros. We deform the path such that it makes an arbitrarily small circle $C_{\alpha}$ around each zero and retraces its path between zeros, such that we obtain a sum of contour integrals around each zero. Near a zero at $\mathsf{k}_{\alpha}$ with multiplicity $p_{\alpha}$ we have that $U_{\mathsf{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1},\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})\propto(\mathsf{k}-\mathsf{k}_{\alpha})^{p_{\alpha}}$ , which implies

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial\mathrm{BZ}}\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\ln\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1}\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})d\mathsf{k} \displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{C_{\alpha}}p_{\alpha}\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\ln(\mathsf{k}-\mathsf{k}_{\alpha}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}=N_{z}. $$

We now compute (98) directly on the boundary of the Brillouin Zone using ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -space boundary conditions to relate it to the Chern number of the band. Specifically, we have that $\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}}$ is related by a gauge transformation $\Xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\mathsf{k})$ , a matrix in band space, to $e^{-i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}$ :

$$ \mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}}=\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}(\mathsf{k})e^{-i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}. $$

For the function (96) we have

$$ \mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}}(\{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{a}\})=\det\Xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\mathsf{k})e^{-i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot\sum_{a}{\boldsymbol{r}}_{a}}\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}(\{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{a}\}). $$

We may then directly compute the contour integrate around the parallelogram ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ , ${\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}$ , ${\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}$ , and ${\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}$ as

$$ \displaystyle 2\pi iN_{z} \displaystyle=\oint_{\partial\mathrm{BZ}}\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\ln\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1}\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})d\mathsf{k} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{1}}^{\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{1}+\mathsf{G}_{2}}\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}(\mathsf{k}-\mathsf{G}_{1}) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{1}+\mathsf{G}_{2}}^{\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{2}}\partial_{\mathsf{k}}\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}(\mathsf{k}-\mathsf{G}_{2})d\mathsf{k} \displaystyle=\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}(\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{2})-\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}(\mathsf{k}) \displaystyle+\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}(\mathsf{k})-\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}(\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{1}). $$

Note that the dependence of the boundary conditions (100) on ${\boldsymbol{r}}_{a}$ has dropped out due to the derivative $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}$ .

We now compute the Chern number of the vortexable band using the boundary conditions (99). First we deal with the fact that our choice of holomorphic gauge has resulted in non-orthonormal band basis. The usual definition of the Berry connection ${\boldsymbol{A}}_{ab}=-i\bra{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}b}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ is not valid in this setting: it is only gauge covariant under unitary gauge transformations. There is a simple fix, however, through the use of the Gram matrix $X_{ab}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\bra{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}b}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}$ which transforms as $X({\boldsymbol{k}})\to S_{\boldsymbol{k}}X({\boldsymbol{k}})S_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}$ for general invertible $S_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ The Berry connection

$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_{ab}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-i(\bra{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}}X^{-1})_{b}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{u_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}}, $$

transforms as

$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\to S^{-1}_{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}})S_{\boldsymbol{k}}-iS^{-1}_{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}S_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$

under a general invertible gauge transformation $S_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ . Thus, under ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}$ we have, using the holomorphic gauge $\ket{\mathsf{u}_{\mathsf{k}}}$ and the associated boundary conditions (99),

$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}})=\Xi^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}(\mathsf{k}){\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\Xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\mathsf{k})-i\Xi^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}(\mathsf{k}){\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\mathsf{k}) $$

such that

$$ \displaystyle\tr({\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}})-{\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}})) \displaystyle=-i\tr\Xi^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}(\mathsf{k}){\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\mathsf{k}) \displaystyle=-i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\tr\log\Xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\mathsf{k}) \displaystyle=-i{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\log\det\Xi_{\boldsymbol{G}}(\mathsf{k}). $$

We now compute the Chern number, which in our smooth non-periodic gauge can be obtained via Stokes’ theorem

$$ \displaystyle 2\pi iC \displaystyle=i\int_{\mathrm{BZ}}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathcal{F}({\boldsymbol{k}}) \displaystyle=i\oint_{\partial\mathrm{BZ}}{\boldsymbol{A}}\cdot d{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle=i\int_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}^{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-{\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}))\cdot d{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle+i\int_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}^{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}})-{\boldsymbol{A}}({\boldsymbol{k}}-{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2})\cdot d{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle=\int_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}^{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}(\mathsf{k}-\mathsf{G}_{1})\cdot d{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle+\int_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}^{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}{\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}(\mathsf{k}-\mathsf{G}_{2})\cdot d{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle=\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}(\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{2})-\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{1}}(\mathsf{k}) \displaystyle+\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}(\mathsf{k})-\ln\det\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{G}}_{2}}(\mathsf{k}+\mathsf{G}_{1}). $$

Comparing (106) and (101) yields our desired result. ∎

We are now in a position to state and prove our uniqueness result.

#### Proposition 3.

A vortexable band with discrete translation symmetry ${\boldsymbol{r}}\to{\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}}$ , $\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}=\partial_{\mu}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})$ and an electron density $\rho({\boldsymbol{r}})=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}\lvert\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}a}({\boldsymbol{r}})\rvert^{2}$ that is finite, continuous, and almost never zero, has a unique vortex function up to affine transformations $\mathsf{z}\to\alpha\mathsf{z}+\beta$ .

#### Proof.

In this proof we will restrict to $C,\Omega>0$ without loss of generality (note that for $C=0$ the assumption that the electron density is finite and continuous is false: see Sec. A.1).

Let us assume that there are two vortex functions $\mathsf{z}_{1}$ and $\mathsf{z}_{2}$ (which we will eventually show must be related by an affine transformation) that satisfy

$$ \mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\omega^{(1)}_{\mu}a^{\mu},\quad\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\omega^{(2)}_{\mu}a^{\mu}. $$

By Prop 2, we have periodic wavefunctions

$$ \ket{\mathsf{u}^{(i)}_{\mathsf{k}^{(i)}}}=S_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{(i)}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}_{i}^{\prime}}\ket{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}, $$

for $i=1,2$ such that $\ket{\mathsf{u}^{(i)}_{\mathsf{k}^{(i)}}}$ is a holomorphic function of $\mathsf{k}^{(i)}=i\left(\Omega^{(\omega_{i})}\right)^{-1}\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\omega_{\mu}^{(i)}k_{\nu}$ and $S_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{(i)}$ is a matrix in band-space that implements the choice of a holomorphic gauge.

The periodic wavefunctions are related as

$$ \ket{\mathsf{u}^{(1)}_{\mathsf{k}_{1}}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1}^{\prime}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{2}^{\prime})}\tilde{S}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\ket{\mathsf{u}^{(2)}_{\mathsf{k}_{2}}}. $$

where $\tilde{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=(S^{(1)}_{\boldsymbol{k}})^{-1}S^{(2)}_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ .

We wish to show that $\omega_{\mu}^{(1)}\propto\omega_{\mu}^{(2)}$ . The intuition is as follows: the shape of the ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -space zeros of $\mathsf{u}^{(1,2)}$ should be similar since they are related linearly as (109). Such zeros must exist due to $C>0$ , which can be justified using Lemma 2. However, the shape of the respective zeros are described by $\omega_{\mu}^{(i)}$ , which should therefore be proportional to each other. The multi-band nature of (109) makes it difficult to immediately conclude this, however, so we pass to “Slater wavefunctions”

$$ \mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}^{(i)}}^{(i)}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1},\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N})=\varepsilon^{a_{1},\ldots a_{N}}\mathsf{u}^{(i)}_{\mathsf{k}a_{1}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1})\ldots\mathsf{u}^{(i)}_{\mathsf{k}a_{N}}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{N}), $$

where $N$ is the number of Bloch bands (that comprise a single vortexable “band”). Using (109) we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}_{1}}^{(1)}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1},\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N}) \displaystyle=\det(\tilde{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}})e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\sum_{a=1}^{N}({\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{a})-{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\prime}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{a}))}\mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}_{2}}^{(2)}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1},\ldots{\boldsymbol{r}}_{N}). $$

Since $C>0$ , Lemma 2 implies that both $\mathsf{U}^{(1)}_{\mathsf{k}_{1}}$ and $\mathsf{U}^{(1)}_{\mathsf{k}_{2}}$ have exactly $C$ zeros in the Brilouin zone (we will only focus on one). In fact, due to the proportionality Eq. (111), the set of zeros and their multiplicities is the same for both wavefunctions. These zeros are in general dependent on $\{{\boldsymbol{r}}_{i}\}$ ; the real space coordinates should be understood as fixed in the discussion below. Let us choose one of the zeros ${\boldsymbol{k}}_{0}$ , which has the corresponding complex coordinates $\mathsf{k}^{(i)}_{0}=\mathsf{k}^{(i)}(\boldsymbol{k}_{0})$ . As ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to\boldsymbol{k}_{0}$ , we have

$$ \mathsf{U}_{\mathsf{k}^{(i)}}(\boldsymbol{r}_{1},\dots,\boldsymbol{r}_{N})\propto(\mathsf{k}^{(i)}-\mathsf{k}^{(i)}_{0})^{p}=\left(\epsilon^{\mu\nu}\omega_{\mu}^{(i)}[k_{\nu}-(k_{0})_{\nu}]\right)^{p}. $$

Combining this with Eq. (111) and taking the limit $\boldsymbol{k}\to\boldsymbol{k}_{0}$ , we must have

$$ \frac{\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\omega^{(1)}_{\mu}\delta k_{\nu}}{\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\omega^{(2)}_{\mu}\delta k_{\nu}}=\text{constant}, $$

for all $\delta k_{\nu}=k_{\nu}-k_{0,\nu}$ . This is only possible if $\omega^{(1)}_{\mu}\propto\omega^{(2)}_{\mu}$ , which follows from successively setting $\delta{\boldsymbol{k}}=(1,0)$ and $\delta{\boldsymbol{k}}=(0,1)$ in (113).

We have nowhere set the scale of $\mathsf{z}_{i}$ and $\omega^{(i)}_{\mu}$ , so let us scale the vortex functions $\mathsf{z}_{i}$ by a suitable complex number such that $\omega^{(1)}_{\mu}=\omega^{(2)}_{\mu}=\omega_{\mu}$ and $\mathsf{k}_{1}=\mathsf{k}_{2}=\mathsf{k}$ . The relationship (109) now takes the form

$$ \ket{\mathsf{u}^{(1)}_{\mathsf{k}}}=e^{-i{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{r}}_{1}^{\prime}-{\boldsymbol{r}}_{2}^{\prime})}\tilde{S}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\ket{\mathsf{u}^{(2)}_{\mathsf{k}}}. $$

We act with $\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle 0=i\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\ket{\mathsf{u}^{(1)}_{\mathsf{k}}} \displaystyle=\omega_{\mu}[r_{1}^{\prime\mu}-r_{2}^{\prime\mu}-(\partial^{k_{\mu}}\tilde{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}})\tilde{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{-1}\ket{\mathsf{u}^{(1)}_{\mathsf{k}}} \displaystyle=(\mathsf{z}_{1}-\mathsf{z}_{2}-T_{\boldsymbol{k}})\ket{\mathsf{u}^{(1)}_{\mathsf{k}}}, $$

where we set $T_{\boldsymbol{k}}=(\overline{\partial}_{\mathsf{k}}\tilde{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}})\tilde{S}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{-1}$ .

We wish to show that $T_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ must be diagonalizable. Suppose not, and consider a sufficiently small region $B$ of ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -space such that the eigenvalues of $T_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ , $\lambda_{i}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ , remain fixed in number and do not have crossings. Then we have a Jordan decomposition $T_{\boldsymbol{k}}=V_{\boldsymbol{k}}M_{\boldsymbol{k}}V_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{-1}$ where

$$ M=\diag\begin{pmatrix}M_{\lambda_{1}},M_{\lambda_{2}},\dots\end{pmatrix}\text{where }M_{\lambda}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&0&0&\cdots\\
1&\lambda&0&\cdots\\
0&1&\lambda&\cdots\\
\vdots&&&\ddots&\end{pmatrix}. $$

Let us focus on a single Jordan block of size $D\times D$ associated to an eigenvalue $\lambda({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . We assume and soon contradict $D>1$ . Put $\ket{\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}=V_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{\mathsf{u}^{(1)}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ . Then in this block we have

$$ 0=\big[\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}})\big]\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},i}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\sum_{j}M_{ij}({\boldsymbol{k}})\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},j}({\boldsymbol{r}}) $$

for $1\leq i\leq D$ . For $i=1$ , using the Jordan form (116) we have

$$ 0=\left[\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\lambda({\boldsymbol{k}})\right]\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},1}({\boldsymbol{r}}). $$

such that whenever $\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},1}({\boldsymbol{r}})\neq 0$ , for ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ in our restricted region $B$ , we have $\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\lambda({\boldsymbol{k}})=\lambda$ .

The equation for $i=2$ yields

$$ 0=\left[\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\lambda({\boldsymbol{k}})\right]\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},2}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},1}({\boldsymbol{r}}) $$

The result (119), together with (118), implies that $D=1$ such that $M$ is diagonal: indeed, choose some ${\boldsymbol{r}}={\boldsymbol{r}}_{0}$ for which $\tilde{u}^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}_{0},1}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})\neq 0$ . Then using (118) we may set $\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}}_{0})-\lambda({\boldsymbol{k}})=0$ in (119) which contradicts our assumption that $M$ has a Jordan block of size larger than $1$ .

We may then take $M=\diag(\lambda_{1}({\boldsymbol{k}}),\ldots,\lambda_{N}({\boldsymbol{k}}))$ . For any ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ for which the density $\rho({\boldsymbol{r}})\neq 0$ , which almost all ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ by assumption, there is a neighborhood of ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ (by continuity) such that $u^{(1)}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}i}({\boldsymbol{r}})\neq 0$ . Using (117) for this $i$ we conclude $\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\lambda_{i}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ , or alternatively ${\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}(\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}}))=0$ for almost all ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ . Continuous functions cannot differ only on measure zero sets of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ so we must have ${\boldsymbol{\nabla}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}(\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}}))=0$ for all ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ such that $\mathsf{z}_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})-\mathsf{z}_{2}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ differ only by a constant $\lambda$ as claimed. ∎

We now conclude by restricting $\omega_{\mu}$ in systems with discrete $n>2$ fold rotation symmetry.

#### Proposition 4.

Consider a vortexable band with discrete translation symmetry $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+\omega_{\mu}a^{\mu}$ , a finite continuous and generically nonzero electron density, and $C_{n>2}$ fold rotation symmetry. Then we can scale the vortex function such that $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}+{\boldsymbol{a}})=\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})+a_{x}+i\operatorname{sign}(\Omega)a_{y}$

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality we measure ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ from a center of rotation such that ${\boldsymbol{r}}\to C_{n}{\boldsymbol{r}}$ is the vector-action of rotations. From $[\mathcal{P},C_{n}]=0$ , we have that $\mathsf{z}(C_{n}{\boldsymbol{r}})$ is a vortex function if $\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is, such that $\mathsf{z}(C_{n}{\boldsymbol{r}})\propto\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ by uniqueness (Prop 3). Such one dimensional representations of $C_{n}$ are labeled by an angular momentum $m$ , modulo $n$ , that counts the minimum number of times $\mathsf{z}$ winds around $0$ upon a $2\pi$ rotation of ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ . Since $\mathsf{z}$ is injective as a consequence of (5), the angular momentum must be $\pm 1$ . We therefore conclude

$$ \mathsf{z}(C_{n}{\boldsymbol{r}})=e^{\pm 2\pi i/n}\mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{r}}). $$

We will soon see that the $\pm$ sign corresponds to chirality $\operatorname{sign}(\Omega)$ . (This is reasonable because it flips under $\mathsf{z}\to\overline{\mathsf{z}}$ and is positive for $\mathsf{z}=x+iy$ .)

Let us add a constant to $\mathsf{z}$ such that $\mathsf{z}(\boldsymbol{r}=0)=0$ . Then we have, using Prop. 1,

$$ \mathsf{z}({\boldsymbol{a}})=\omega_{\mu}{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\mu}. $$

Combined with (120) we have

$$ \omega_{\mu}(C_{n}{\boldsymbol{a}})^{\mu}=e^{\pm 2\pi i/n}\omega_{\mu}{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\mu} $$

We claim that (122) implies

$$ \omega_{\mu}{\boldsymbol{a}}^{\mu}=\gamma(a_{x}\pm ia_{y}) $$

for some constant $\gamma$ . A geometric picture is helpful here. Consider first the $+$ sign in (122). The complex vector $\omega_{\mu}$ can be understood as a linear map $\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{2}$ that commutes with rotation symmetry (counter-clockwise in both the domain and codomain). If it is not equal to a constant $\gamma$ times the identity, then it has two distinct eigenvectors must be each rotationally invariant which is impossible. For the $(-)$ rep, we may use the same argument above after applying an orientation reversal on one of the domain or codomain.

We now identify the $\pm$ sign in (123) with $\operatorname{sign}(\Omega)$ . This follows from $\operatorname{sign}(-i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu}\overline{\omega_{\mu}}\omega_{\nu})=\pm$ for $\omega=\begin{pmatrix}1&\pm i\end{pmatrix}^{T}$ and the usage of Lemma 1. Then taking $\mathsf{z}\to\mathsf{z}/\gamma$ completes the proof. ∎.
