## Appendix A Symmetries of the chiral model

The main feature of the chiral TBG Hamiltonian is the presence of a chiral or sublattice symmetry which anticommutes with the single-particle Hamiltonian $\{\sigma_{z},H\}=0$ . In addition, weak-spin orbit coupling in graphene implies that $H$ is invariant under ${\rm SU}(2)$ spin rotations, i.e. $H\propto s_{0}$ . The large momentum separation between the graphene valleys leads to valley decoupling at low energies relevant to TBG physics which implies independent spin and charge conservation in each valley i.e. $H$ is diagonal in the valley index $\tau_{z}$ . The two valley are related by spinless time-reversal symmetry which is implemented as $\mathcal{T}=\tau_{x}\mathcal{K}$ with $\mathcal{K}$ denoting complex conjugation, such that $H_{K^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=H_{K}(-{\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}$ . The single particle Hamiltonian is also invariant under two-fold rotation symmetry which flips sublattice and valley $C_{2}=\sigma_{x}\tau_{x}$ . The combination of the two $C_{2}\mathcal{T}=\sigma_{x}\mathcal{K}$ leaves the valley index invariant and relates the two sublattice wavefunctions at the same momentum ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ .

A more subtle symmetry of the chiral TBG Hamiltonian is a particle-hole symmetry $H(-{\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}=\mu_{y}\sigma_{x}H({\boldsymbol{k}})\mu_{y}\sigma_{x}$ where $\mu$ denote the Pauli matrices in layer space [89, 90]. On the level of the single-particle Hamiltonian this is an antiunitary anticommuting symmetry given by $\mathcal{P}=i\mu_{y}\sigma_{x}\mathcal{K}$ whereas in second quantized language, this is a unitary particle-hole symmetry acting as

$$ \mathcal{P}^{-1}f_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}\mathcal{P}=\mu_{y}\sigma_{x}f^{\dagger}_{-{\boldsymbol{k}}},\qquad\mathcal{P}^{-1}i\mathcal{P}=i $$

where $f_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ denotes the annihilation operators for microscopic electrons. In addition to the sublattice, valley, and spin indices, these electrons also carry a layer index.

Since the chiral symmetry $\sigma_{z}$ is anticommuting and unitary ( anti-unitary particle-hole in second quantization), $\mathcal{T}$ is commuting and anti-unitary (anti-unitary in second quantization), and $\mathcal{P}$ is anti-commuting and anti-unitary (unitary particle-hole in second quantization), their product $R=i\sigma_{z}\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}=\tau_{x}\sigma_{y}\mu_{y}$ is a $Z_{2}$ unitary commuting symmetry. This extra “hidden” symmetry relates different valley, sublattice and layer indices and leads to enhanced symmetry of the interacting problem as we will see below.

### A.1 Symmetries and the Form Factor

Let us now see how that symmetries restrict the structure of the form factor $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . Due to the ${\rm SU}(2)$ spin rotation symmetry, the spin index does not play any role in the following discussion so it can be dropped. This essentially corresponds to considering a spinless version of the problem. In the following, we will write out the flat band index $\alpha$ in terms of the sublattice-valley indices $\sigma$ and $\tau$ . We note that sublattice symmetry implies that $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is diagonal in the sublattice index since

$$ \langle u_{A,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{B,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=\langle u_{A,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|\sigma_{z}^{2}|u_{B,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=-\langle u_{A,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{B,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=0 $$

where we used $\sigma_{z}|u_{A/B,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=\pm|u_{A/B,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle$ . In addition, valley symmetry implies that $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is also diagonal in valley. We now note that since $R$ symmetry flips both valley and sublattice, we have

$$ Ru_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=e^{i\phi_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}}u_{-\sigma,-\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}} $$

for some phase $\phi_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ . Since we are free to choose the gauge independently in the two valleys $\tau=\pm=K/K^{\prime}$ and sublattices $\sigma=\pm=A/B$ , we can set $\phi_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ to 0 by fixing the gauge e.g. in valley $K^{\prime}$ relative to $K$ . This means that we can choose the action of $R$ on the flat bands to be $\sigma_{x}\tau_{x}$ 99 9 Note that this gauge choise is slightly different from the one used in Ref. [42]. Similarly, we can deduce the representation of $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ on the flat bands by noting that it flips sublattice but not momentum

$$ C_{2}\mathcal{T}u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=e^{i\eta_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}}u_{-\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{*} $$

The phase factors $\eta_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ are not completely free since we want to preserve the relation $C_{2}\mathcal{T}RC_{2}\mathcal{T}=-R$ satisfied by the microscopic operators which implies that $\eta_{-\sigma,-\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=\eta_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}+\pi$ . Otherwise, we have the freedom to choose the relative phase between the wavefunctions in sublattices A and B such that $\eta_{A,K,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=\eta_{B,K,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=0$ which implies $\eta_{A,K^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{k}}}=\eta_{B,K^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{k}}}=\pi$ . This means that $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ acts as $\sigma_{x}\tau_{z}\mathcal{K}$ in the flat band basis. Note that the action of any of the remaining symmetries, e.g. $\mathcal{T}$ or $C_{2}$ , on the flat band will contain extra phase factors that cannot be removed. In particular, it can be shown that the band topology enforces a non-trivial phase factors for $C_{2}$ symmetry [42].

Using Eq. 118, we can relate the diagonal entries of the form factor between $\sigma,\tau$ and $-\sigma,-\tau$

$$ \langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle=\langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|R^{2}|u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle=\langle u_{-\sigma,-\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{-\sigma,-\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle, $$

This can be used to relate the form factors in opposite valleys at the same momentum. In addition, we can use Eq. 119 to related the form factors within the same valley for the two sublattices leading to

$$ \langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle=\langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|(C_{2}\mathcal{T})^{2}|u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle=\langle u_{-\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{-\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle^{*} $$

Thus, the diagonal entries of the form factor are related by complex conjugation upon exchanging sublattice or valley but remain the same under exchanging both. This leads to the following simple form of the form factor matrix

$$ \Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})e^{i\Phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sigma_{z}\tau_{z}} $$

where $F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ and $\Phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ are scalars. Note that the form factor of a given flat band only depends on the combination $\sigma_{z}\tau_{z}$ which corresponds to the Chern number. This flips under exchanging sublattice (under $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ symmetry), or valley (under $\mathcal{T}$ ) but remains invariant under flipping both (under $C_{2}$ symmetry).

### A.2 Symmetries and the Kinetic Term

Different symmetries restrict the form of the single particle term $h({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . Our main assumption is that, although its value may be renormalized by interactions, it has the same symmetries as the projected chiral BM Hamiltonian (43). First, we can again use spin and valley symmetries to deduce $h({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is proportional to $s_{0}$ and diagonal in valley index. For a single valley, $h({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is stricly off-diagonal in sublattice index since:

$$ \langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|H_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})|u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle=-\langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|\sigma_{z}H_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sigma_{z}|u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle=-\langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|H_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})|u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle=0 $$

This means that the matrix $h({\boldsymbol{k}})$ can only contain the terms $\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{x}\tau_{z}$ , and $\sigma_{y}\tau_{z}$ . We can use the $R$ symmetry to restrict this form further using

$$ \langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|H_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})|u_{\sigma^{\prime},\tau^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle=\langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|RH_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})R|u_{\sigma^{\prime},\tau^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle=\langle u_{-\sigma,-\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|H_{\rm BM}({\boldsymbol{k}})|u_{-\sigma^{\prime},-\tau^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle $$

which implies that $h({\boldsymbol{k}})$ commutes with $\sigma_{x}\tau_{x}$ excluding the terms $\sigma_{y}$ and $\sigma_{x}\tau_{z}$ . This leads to the form

$$ h({\boldsymbol{k}})=h_{x}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sigma_{x}+h_{y}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sigma_{y}\tau_{z} $$

### A.3 Deviations from the chiral limit

Let us now consider what happens when we deviate from the chiral limit $w_{0}=0$ . In this case, chiral symmetry is broken which means that the unitary symmetry $R$ is also broken. As a result, we do not expect the form factors to be diagonal in the sublattice index since the wavefunctions are no longer completely sublattice polarized. We can still use valley and spin symmetries to show that the form factor is diagonal in valley and proportional to the identity in spin space.

To restrict the form factor further, we note that the particle-hole symmetry $\mathcal{P}$ remains a symmetry to a good approximation provided we assume the angle is small 1010 10 it is only a symmetry if we ignore the angular rotation in the Pauli matrices in Eq. 3 which is equivalent to the replacemntsuch that $\sigma_{\pm\theta/2}\mapsto\sigma$ . We note that the product of $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ anticommutes with the single particle Hamiltonian which means that the action of $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}=\mu_{y}\tau_{x}\sigma_{x}$ maps positive energy states to negative energy states at the same momentum ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ . As a result, it leave the space of flat bands invariant and we can write

$$ \mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=e^{i\varphi_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}}u_{-\sigma,-\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}} $$

To be compatible with the gauge choice in Appendix A.1, we choose the gauge such that $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}=i\sigma_{z}R=\sigma_{y}\tau_{x}$ which implies that the form factor satisfies $\sigma_{y}\tau_{x}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sigma_{y}\tau_{x}=\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . This restricts the form factor to the terms $\tau_{0}\sigma_{0,y}$ and $\tau_{z}\sigma_{x,z}$ . In addition, we can use $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ (cf. Eq. 119) to get

$$ \langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{\sigma^{\prime},\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle=\langle u_{\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|(C_{2}\mathcal{T})^{2}|u_{\sigma^{\prime},\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle=\langle u_{-\sigma,\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|u_{-\sigma^{\prime},\tau,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle^{*} $$

which yields $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\sigma_{x}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{*}\sigma_{x}$ which implies that the coefficients of $\tau_{0}\sigma_{0}$ , $\tau_{0}\sigma_{x}$ and $\tau_{z}\sigma_{y}$ are real while the coefficient of $\tau_{z}\sigma_{z}$ is imaginary leading to the form

$$ \Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})e^{i\Phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sigma_{z}\tau_{z}}+\sigma_{x}\tau_{z}\tilde{F}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})e^{i\tilde{\Phi}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sigma_{z}\tau_{z}} $$

Compared to Eq. 122, there is an extra sublattice off-diagonal term which is only non-vanishing away from the chiral limit.

## Appendix B Perturbative correction to energy due to single-particle disperison $h$

To compute the perturbative correction to energy due to single-particle dispersion $h$ , we write $\Delta E=J({\boldsymbol{n}}_{+}\cdot{\boldsymbol{n}}_{-}-1)$ and take ${\boldsymbol{n}}_{+}=-{\boldsymbol{n}}_{-}=\hat{z}$ . We see that the contribution from the tunneling $\Delta E$ is equal to twice the contribution from tunneling connecting a single fully filled Chern band to a single fully empty band in the opposite Chern sector. This means we can restrict ourselves to a pair of tunnel-coupled opposite Chern bands and just multiply the result by 2 1111 11 the factor of 2 cancels out due to our definition of $J$ with $\Delta E=-2J$ such that the absolute value of the result is precisely J. For definiteness, we take the positive Chern band to be fully filled and the negative Chern band to be fully empty such that the total number of electrons in the $\pm$ band is $N_{+}=N$ and $N_{-}=0$ . The single particle “tunneling” term has the form

$$ \hat{h}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}c_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}h({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}c_{+,{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{\dagger}[h_{x}({\boldsymbol{k}})-ih_{y}({\boldsymbol{k}})]c_{-,{\boldsymbol{k}}}+\text{h.c.} $$

where $c_{\boldsymbol{k}}=(c_{+,{\boldsymbol{k}}},c_{-,{\boldsymbol{k}}})$ is a 2-component vector with annihilation operators in the $\pm$ Chern band. $\hat{h}$ does not conserve the particle number in each Chern sector separately. Acting with in on a state with $(N_{+},N_{-})=(N,0)$ yields a state with $(N_{+},N_{-})=(N-1,1)$ with an electron hole pair at some momentum ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ which can be written as

$$ |\Psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}\rangle=c^{\dagger}_{-,{\boldsymbol{k}}}c_{+,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|\Psi_{0}\rangle $$

The interacting part of the Hamiltonian conserves momentum and Chern number so it maps the state $|\Psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}\rangle$ to a state $|\Psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle$ and it determines the energy spectrum of the particle-hole excitations. As a result, the second order correction to the energy can be written as

$$ \Delta E=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}[h_{x}({\boldsymbol{k}})+ih_{y}({\boldsymbol{k}})][\mathcal{H}_{\rm eh}]_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}^{-1}[h_{x}({\boldsymbol{k}})-ih_{y}({\boldsymbol{k}})], $$

with $\mathcal{H}_{\rm eh}$ given by [42]

$$ [\mathcal{H}_{\rm eh}]_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\langle\Psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}|\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}\delta\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}|\Psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\rangle=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{2}[\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}-\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},[{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}]}e^{2i\Phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})}] $$

where $[{\boldsymbol{q}}]$ denotes the part of ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ within the first Moiré Brillouin zone.
